planting.note: Plant divisions or container starts in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to a few hours of morning sun; space 12-18 inches apart, since this cultivar spreads by surface stolons and fills in faster than most other tricolor ajugas.

directions: Ajuga reptans 'Multicolor' produces dense, glossy rosettes patterned in bronze-green, cream, and dusky pink, with the variegation intensifying in cool spring and autumn weather. Short spikes of blue-violet flowers rise above the foliage in late spring, drawing early pollinators to the shade garden. It spreads by surface stolons into a tight, weed-resistant mat somewhat more vigorously than 'Burgundy Glow' already in this dataset, and it holds its variegated color across a wider range of light exposures than most patterned ajugas, from partial shade into a few hours of direct sun.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Set divisions or nursery starts in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; its dense, fast-filling habit makes it effective for closing gaps quickly along shaded walkways and under trees.

directions: Ajuga reptans 'Blueberry Muffin' forms a compact, tightly knit mat of small, glossy, bronze-flushed green leaves that stay noticeably smaller and denser than those of 'Chocolate Chip' already in this dataset. In mid-spring it sends up short spikes of vivid deep blue flowers that make a strong color statement against the dark foliage. Its faster fill rate and dense habit help it outcompete weeds and hold soil on shaded slopes better than looser-growing ajuga selections.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade; established clumps tolerate drier shade under trees better than most foamflowers, though flowering and fall color are best with consistent moisture.

directions: Tiarella cordifolia 'Brandywine' bears deeply lobed, glossy, rugose leaves marked with a bold burgundy central pattern that deepens into bronze-red tones through fall and winter. Creamy white bottlebrush flower spikes rise well above the foliage for several weeks in mid-spring, a longer bloom display than many other foamflower selections. It forms a robust clump that sends out modest stolons in spring and fall, spreading gradually rather than aggressively, and tolerates drier shade once established better than most foamflowers in this dataset.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Eco Red Heart Foamflower (Red-Centered Native Foamflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; it spreads readily by surface stolons and colonizes bare ground under trees within a couple of growing seasons.

directions: Tiarella cordifolia 'Eco Red Heart' was selected by Don Jacobs of Eco Gardens for the vivid burgundy-red blotch that fills the center of each rounded, lightly lobed leaf, a bolder and more solidly colored central marking than the fine veining typical of the wild species. Fragrant white star-shaped flowers rise just above the foliage on short stalks in spring. Like the species, it spreads readily by surface stolons to form a dense colony, making it useful as a naturalizing native groundcover under deciduous trees.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Berries and Cream Pulmonaria (Bicolor Raspberry-Pink Silver-Spotted Lungwort)

planting.note: Divide established clumps just after flowering or in early fall and plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this Terra Nova introduction shows better resistance to powdery mildew than many older lungwort cultivars.

directions: Pulmonaria 'Berries and Cream' carries large, ruffled, heavily silver-splashed leaves that form a mounding basal clump wider than it is tall. In early spring, drooping clusters of funnel-shaped flowers open raspberry-pink and deepen toward purple as they age, giving the plant a two-toned, berry-like flower display. It shows better resistance to powdery mildew than many older lungwort cultivars, allowing its silvered foliage to stay attractive through summer shade.

common_name: Shrimps on the Barbie Lungwort (Coral-Pink Silver-Spotted Pulmonaria)

planting.note: Divide clumps after flowering and plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; cutting back tired foliage after bloom encourages a fresh flush of clean, silver-spotted leaves for summer.

directions: Pulmonaria 'Shrimps on the Barbie' bears long, densely silver-spotted leaves and produces an unusually heavy flush of large, deep shrimp-pink flowers in early spring, a stronger bloom display than most silver-leaved lungworts already in this dataset. Its foliage stays clean and notably mildew-resistant through the growing season, remaining attractive well past the spring bloom period. Cutting back tired leaves after flowering encourages a fresh flush of foliage for summer.

common_name: Polar Splash Pulmonaria (Heavily Silver-Spotted Sun-Tolerant Lungwort)

planting.note: Divide clumps after flowering and plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; this cultivar tolerates brighter exposures than most lungworts, but foliage quality is still best with consistent moisture and afternoon shade.

directions: Pulmonaria 'Polar Splash' produces broad leaves almost entirely overlaid in silvery-white spotting, leaving only narrow margins of green visible, among the most heavily marked foliage of any lungwort in this dataset. Clusters of flowers open pink and mature to violet-blue on the same plant, creating a two-toned display in early to mid-spring. It tolerates noticeably more sun than most pulmonaria cultivars without scorching, though foliage quality remains best with consistent moisture and some afternoon shade.
